title: Ser, estar and how you feel
objectives: I can ask and answer Como você está? and say how I feel.
I can explain why estou, está, estão, simpático and similar words are spelled and stressed the way they are.
I can describe people with adjectives that agree in gender and number.
I can choose between ser and estar by asking whether I am classifying something or describing its place or condition.
I can say what my job is and ask what other people do.
I can make negative sentences with não, answer yes or no questions by repeating the verb, and ask questions with quem, como, onde and o que.

vocabulary.note: The second Portuguese verb for to be. Ser says what something is; estar says where it is and what condition it is in at the moment. It comes from Latin stare, to stand. Es-TAR ends in r, so by the default rule the stress is on the last syllable and no accent is needed. The present forms are estou, está, estamos and estão.

Feminine: cansada. The an before s ends a syllable, so the a is nasal: kan-SA-du, with the final o said u. The stress is on the second to last syllable, the default for a word ending in o, so there is no accent.

Same form for men and women; plural: felizes. A word ending in z is stressed on the last syllable by default (fe-LIZ), so no accent is needed. The final z is said s in São Paulo and sh in Rio; in felizes the z sits between vowels and is said z.
Same form for men and women. The final e is weak and said i, so the t before it is said tch: TRIS-tchi. The tr is a tap, as in prato.

An adverb, so it never changes for gender or number: men and women both say Estou bem. Final em is a nasal vowel, said like ayn through the nose, and the lips do not close for the m. Estou bem is the standard way to say you are fine.
The opposite of bem and also an adverb, so it never changes. With estar it means unwell. The l at the end of a syllable is said w, so mal is said MAW, like the start of English mouse.

Portuguese names the feeling with a noun: you are with hunger, where English uses the adjective hungry. Because fome is a noun, it never changes for gender: Ela está com fome. Always estar, never ser. The o of fome is closed and the final e is said i: FO-mi.
Sono is the noun sleep, so there is no agreement. In com the m only nasalizes the o and the lips do not close: kõ. The stressed o of sono is closed: SO-nu.
Sede is a noun, so there is no agreement. The d comes before the weak final e, which is said i, so the d is said dj: SE-dji, with a closed e.

Same form for men and women. Oe is two strong vowels side by side, which never form a diphthong, so the word has three syllables: do-EN-te. The en before t is nasal and the t before the final e is said tch.
Feminine: ocupada. The c before u is said k: o-ku-PA-du. The stress is on the second to last syllable, the default for a word ending in o.
Feminine: alta. The l at the end of a syllable is said w: AW-tu. Used with ser, because height is part of what a person is.

Feminine: simpática. It is stressed on the third syllable from the end (sim-PA-tchi-ku), which no ending predicts, so it is always written with an accent; the a is open, so the accent is acute. The im is nasal and the t before i is said tch. It looks like sympathetic but means pleasant and likeable, not feeling sorry for someone.

Same form for men and women. G before e is said zh, the final e is said i and so the t before it is said tch: in-te-li-ZHEN-tchi. The stress is on the second to last syllable, the default for a word ending in e.
Feminine: engraçada. Built on graça, charm or wit. The ç is said s before a, and a ç never starts a word: en-gra-SA-du, with a nasal en.
Feminine: bonita. Related to bom, good. Used for people and things. With ser it says how someone looks; with estar it says how they look at a particular moment.

Feminine: a professora; nouns in -or add -a. The ss between vowels is s (a single s there would be z). A word ending in r is stressed on the last syllable by default (pro-fes-SOR), so there is no accent; professora follows the default for a and is stressed on the second to last.

Feminine: a médica. Stressed on the third syllable from the end, so it is always written with an accent, acute because the e is open. The accent stays in médica and médicos. The d before i is said dj: MÉ-dji-ku.
Feminine: a engenheira. The en is nasal, g before e is zh, nh is ny as in banho, and ei is the vowel of day: en-zhe-NYEI-ru.
Same form for both genders; the article shows which: o estudante, a estudante. Nouns in -ante have no separate feminine form. The an is nasal and the t before the final e is said tch.
Masculine: o enfermeiro. En before f is nasal, the r closes the syllable fer, and ei is a diphthong: en-fer-MEI-ra.
Asks about people. In quem the qu before e is said k with a silent u, and the final em is a nasal vowel, said like ayn through the nose.
The stressed o is closed: KO-mu. Como é ele? asks what he is like; Como ele está? asks how he is right now.
The on before d is nasal, and the d before the weak final e is said dj: ON-dji.
Two words, used together at the start of a question. In que, qu before e is k with a silent u, and the unstressed e is said i: u ki.
A neutral pointing word: it does not change for gender or number, and it refers to a thing or to what was just said. The ss between vowels is s; a single s there would be z: IS-su.
Before an adjective or adverb it is an adverb and never changes: muito cansado, muito cansada. The ui is a diphthong, and the m before it nasalizes it even though no tilde is written: MUI-tu.
Qu before i is said k with a silent u. It ends in i, so the default puts the stress on the last syllable, a-KI, and no accent is needed. An adverb of place, so it never changes.
No article is used in this phrase. Em before a noun means in or at. The c before a is k, and the single s between vowels is z: KA-za.

The tilde makes the vowel nasal: nãw, like English now said through the nose. The ending ão is stressed on the last syllable by default, so no accent is needed. Goes directly before the verb to make it negative.
The h is always silent and j is always zh: O-zhi, with a closed o and a final e said i. An adverb of time, so it never changes.
The h is silent and the l at the end of a syllable is said w: os-pi-TAW. A word ending in l is stressed on the last syllable by default. With em it contracts: no hospital is em + o.
The s at the end of a syllable is s in São Paulo and sh in Rio. Do not confuse it with mais, more, which has the diphthong ai.

Said when answering or starting a phone call. Related to English hello. It is a-LÔ: a word ending in o defaults to the second to last syllable, the stress is on the last, so an accent is written, and a circumflex because the o is closed, as in avô.
Que before a noun in an exclamation means what a. Said to show sympathy or regret. Pena is pity or sorrow, PE-na with a closed e. Que is said ki, as in o que.

example.en: What a pity! You are sick.

dialogues.title: How are you today?
dialogues.context: Ana and Carlos meet in the street near the hospital. Ana is in the middle of a long day at work.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Oi, Carlos! Como você está?
lines.en: Hi, Carlos! How are you?
lines.literal: Hi, Carlos! How you are?

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: Oi, Ana! Estou bem, obrigado. E você?
lines.en: Hi, Ana! I am fine, thank you. And you?
lines.literal: Hi, Ana! I-am well, obliged. And you?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Estou muito cansada. Estou com sono.
lines.en: I am very tired. I am sleepy.
lines.literal: I-am very tired. I-am with sleep.

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: Você está ocupada hoje?
lines.en: Are you busy today?
lines.literal: You are busy today?

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Estou, sim. Sou enfermeira e estou no hospital hoje.
lines.en: Yes, I am. I am a nurse and I am at the hospital today.
lines.literal: I-am, yes. I-am nurse and I-am in-the hospital today.

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: Enfermeira? Que legal! Eu sou professor.
lines.en: A nurse? How cool! I am a teacher.
lines.literal: Nurse? What cool! I am teacher.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Professor? Você não é engenheiro?
lines.en: A teacher? Aren't you an engineer?
lines.literal: Teacher? You not are engineer?

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: Não, eu não sou engenheiro. Sou professor.
lines.en: No, I am not an engineer. I am a teacher.
lines.literal: No, I not am engineer. I-am teacher.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.pt: Desculpa, Carlos! Hoje estou muito cansada.
lines.en: Sorry, Carlos! Today I am very tired.
lines.literal: Excuse, Carlos! Today I-am very tired.

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: Tudo bem, Ana. Até logo!
lines.en: That's fine, Ana. See you later!
lines.literal: All well, Ana. Until soon!

dialogues.title: Who is that?
dialogues.context: Pedro and Marina are at a party. Pedro asks Marina about two people he does not know.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Marina, quem é ele?
lines.en: Marina, who is he?

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.pt: Ele é o Rafael, um amigo.
lines.en: He is Rafael, a friend.
lines.literal: He is the Rafael, a friend.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Ele é engenheiro?
lines.en: Is he an engineer?
lines.literal: He is engineer?

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.pt: É, sim. E é muito simpático e engraçado.
lines.en: Yes, he is. And he is very nice and funny.
lines.literal: Is, yes. And is very nice and funny.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: E ela? Quem é ela?
lines.en: And her? Who is she?

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.pt: Ela é a Paula. Ela é médica.
lines.en: She is Paula. She is a doctor.
lines.literal: She is the Paula. She is doctor.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Ela é muito bonita! E alta.
lines.en: She is very pretty! And tall.

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.pt: É, e é muito inteligente também.
lines.en: Yes, and she is very intelligent too.
lines.literal: Is, and is very intelligent too.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.pt: Onde ela está?
lines.en: Where is she?
lines.literal: Where she is?

lines.speaker: Marina
lines.pt: Ela está aqui, com o Rafael.
lines.en: She is here, with Rafael.
lines.literal: She is here, with the Rafael.

dialogues.title: A phone call to a sick friend
dialogues.context: Camila calls her friend Bruno, who did not go to work today.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: Alô, Bruno! Onde você está?
lines.en: Hello, Bruno! Where are you?
lines.literal: Hello, Bruno! Where you are?

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.pt: Oi, Camila! Estou em casa. Hoje eu estou doente.
lines.en: Hi, Camila! I am at home. Today I am sick.
lines.literal: Hi, Camila! I-am in house. Today I am sick.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: Que pena! Como você está?
lines.en: What a pity! How are you?
lines.literal: What pity! How you are?

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.pt: Estou mal, mas não estou triste.
lines.en: I am unwell, but I am not sad.
lines.literal: I-am badly, but not I-am sad.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: Você está com fome?
lines.en: Are you hungry?
lines.literal: You are with hunger?

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.pt: Estou, sim! E também estou com sede.
lines.en: Yes, I am! And I am also thirsty.
lines.literal: I-am, yes! And also I-am with thirst.

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: Eu não sou médica, mas sou amiga.
lines.en: I am not a doctor, but I am a friend.
lines.literal: I not am doctor, but I-am friend.

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.pt: Você é muito simpática, Camila. Obrigado!
lines.en: You are very nice, Camila. Thank you!
lines.literal: You are very nice, Camila. Obliged!

lines.speaker: Camila
lines.pt: De nada! Tchau, Bruno.
lines.en: You're welcome! Bye, Bruno.
lines.literal: Of nothing! Bye, Bruno.

lines.speaker: Bruno
lines.pt: Tchau!
lines.en: Bye!

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: reading the words of this unit
grammar.explanation:
Every word in this unit can be read with the rules from the first three lessons. Nothing here needs a new rule, only practice in applying the old ones, and the lesson is easier if you do the same four steps every time. First, divide the word into syllables. Second, find the stressed syllable by ear. Third, read the default stress from the ending: a word ending in a, e or o (with or without a final s), am, em or ens is stressed on the second to last syllable, and a word ending in anything else is stressed on the last syllable. Fourth, if the real stress breaks the default, the stressed vowel carries a written accent, acute for an open vowel and circumflex for a closed one. Then read each letter by the sound rules: a final unstressed o is said u and a final unstressed e is said i; t and d before the sound i become tch and dj; l at the end of a syllable is w; a vowel followed by an m or n that ends the syllable is nasal; h is silent.

The forms of estar are the best practice, because the same rules explain every accent and tilde on them. Estar is es-TAR. It ends in r, so the default is the last syllable and no accent is needed. Estou is es-TOW: ou is a diphthong, which is one syllable, and the default for a diphthong ending is the last syllable, so again no accent. Está is es-TÁ: it ends in a, so the default would be ES-ta, but the stress is on the last syllable, so the stressed vowel is marked, and acute because the a is open. That one accent is the only difference between está (is) and esta (this, said ES-ta). Estamos ends in os, so it is stressed on the second to last by default, es-TA-mus, and needs nothing; its a is slightly nasal only because an m follows it. Estão ends in ão, a default-last ending: the tilde makes the vowel nasal, and because no other accent is present, the tilde also marks the stress, es-TÃO, like English now said through the nose. In all of these the first syllable is weak: the e at the start of a word before s is often said i, and the s at the end of a syllable is s in São Paulo and sh in Rio, so estar can sound like is-TAR or esh-TAR.

Brazilians shorten estar in fast speech by dropping the weak first syllable: estou becomes tô, está becomes tá, estão becomes tão. What remains is one stressed syllable, and lesson 2 gave the rule for that: a stressed one-syllable word ending in a, e or o is written with an accent. So tá has an acute (open a) and tô a circumflex (closed o, like the o of go without the glide). The tilde of tão is the same as in estão.

Adjectives and professions show the other patterns. Simpático and médico are stressed on the third syllable from the end. No ending predicts that stress, so such words are always accented, and the vowel quality chooses the mark: open a and open e take the acute. The accent stays in simpática and médicas, because the stress stays on the same syllable. Alô is a-LÔ: it ends in o, so the default would be A-lo, and the stress on the last syllable needs a circumflex because the o is closed, exactly as in avô. Doente has two strong vowels side by side, o and e, and two strong vowels never make a diphthong, so it has three syllables, do-EN-te. Nasal vowels appear in cansado, doente, inteligente, estudante, engenheiro, enfermeira, onde, simpático, bem, quem, com, muito and não: whenever m or n closes a syllable, it is not said as a consonant but turns the vowel before it nasal. A tilde is written only on a and o, and only where no m or n does the job. In bem and quem the final em is said like ayn through the nose. Muito is a spelling exception: no tilde is written, but the m still nasalizes the diphthong ui.

The consonants follow the position rules. G before e is zh (inteligente, engenheiro), ç is s before a (engraçado), qu before e is k with a silent u (quem, que), nh is ny (engenheiro), h is silent (hoje, hospital), ss between vowels is s while a single s there is z (isso against casa), l at the end of a syllable is w (alto, mal, hospital, Rafael), t before an i sound is tch and d before an i sound is dj (triste, doente, estudante, onde, sede, médico). An unstressed final e counts as an i sound, which is why the t of triste and the d of onde change.

grammar.title: Ser and estar in the present: two verbs for to be
grammar.explanation:
English has one verb, to be, for every job: I am a teacher, I am tired, I am in Rio. Portuguese splits the work between two verbs, ser and estar. Spanish and Galician make the same split, so this is an ordinary feature of the Iberian languages, not a peculiarity of Portuguese. Both verbs are irregular, which in this course means they do not follow the stem plus ending pattern of a regular family, so each form is learned as it is. They are irregular because they are among the commonest verbs in the language, and the commonest words keep the oldest and most worn forms.

The split is old. Ser comes from two Latin verbs, esse (to be) and sedere (to sit). Estar comes from stare, to stand. The idea of standing explains what estar still does: it says that something is in a place or in a condition at some moment, as if it were standing there. Ser says what something is. That picture is not a rule, but it is the logic behind the rules in the next note.

The forms are few. In Brazil você, ele, ela and a gente share one form, because você is grammatically third person (lesson 3), and vocês, eles and elas share another. So each verb has four forms: sou, é, somos, são and estou, está, estamos, estão. Look at the stress. In a regular verb the stem carries the stress in these forms (FA-lo, FA-la, FA-lam), but in estou, está and estão the stress jumps to the ending: es-TOW, es-TÁ, es-TÃO. That jump is the irregularity, and the written accent on está and the tilde on estão record it. Estamos is es-TA-mus, with the stress where a regular verb would put it.

In everyday speech estar is shortened by dropping its weak first syllable: tô, tá, tão, and for we also tamos. English does the same with I'm, he's and they're. Tá is also used alone as okay, as in Tá bem or just Tá. Ser is not shortened in this way, and there is a reason: sou, é and são are already one syllable, and in somos the first syllable is the stressed one, so there is nothing weak to drop. Write the full forms when you write carefully, and expect to hear the short ones.

grammar.title: Choosing between ser and estar: classifying versus describing a condition
grammar.explanation:
The principle is that the two verbs answer two different questions. Ser links the subject to what it is: its identity, its origin, its profession, its qualities as part of what it is. Estar links the subject to its circumstances: where it is, and what condition it is in. A common rule of thumb says ser is for permanent things and estar for temporary ones. It works often, but it is not the real rule, and it fails in both directions. A person's job can change, and it still takes ser, because it classifies the person. A mood can last all week, and it still takes estar, because it describes a condition. Ask instead: am I saying what this is, or how and where it is at the moment?

Use ser for identity (Eu sou o Paulo), origin (Ela é do Brasil), profession (Ele é médico) and qualities seen as part of the person (Ela é alta, ele é simpático). With a profession Portuguese drops the article: Sou professor, not Sou um professor. The profession works like an adjective here, naming a class the person belongs to, while English needs a. When the profession is described further, the article returns as in English: Ela é uma médica simpática, She is a nice doctor.

Use estar for the place of a person or thing (Estou em casa, Ela está no hospital) and for conditions: feelings, moods, health and how you are at the moment (Estou cansado, Ele está triste). Como você está? asks how you are now. Estou bem and Estou mal use bem and mal, which are adverbs: an adverb is a word that tells how, when, where or how much, and it modifies a verb, an adjective or another adverb. Adverbs never agree with anything, so men and women both say Estou bem.

Physical needs are expressed differently from English. English uses an adjective (hungry, thirsty, sleepy); Portuguese says you are with the thing: estar com fome, com sede, com sono (and with the same pattern com frio, cold, and com calor, hot). Fome, sede and sono are nouns, so they never agree with the subject: Ela está com fome, Elas estão com sono. Always estar, never ser, because hunger is a condition you are in.

The same adjective can go with either verb, and the meaning changes with the question being answered. Ele é feliz says he is a happy person. Ele está feliz says he is happy at this moment. Ela é bonita says she is pretty; Ela está bonita says she looks pretty today. English has no matching choice in the verb and must add words such as looks or is being.

One exception is worth knowing early. The place of an event takes ser: A festa é em casa, The party is at home. The location says where the event happens, which is part of what the event is, not where an object is sitting. Finally, a place is introduced by em, which fuses with the article in the usual way: em + o = no (no hospital) and em + a = na (na escola, at school). There is no article in em casa, so nothing fuses.

rows: Place of a person or thing

grammar.title: Adjective agreement and professions
grammar.explanation:
In Portuguese, a word that describes a noun copies its gender and number. This copying is called agreement, and it is what makes the language hang together. After ser and estar the adjective stands after the verb, but it still describes the subject and still agrees with it. Estou cansado is said by a man and Estou cansada by a woman. A group of women says Estamos cansadas; a group of men, or men and women together, says Estamos cansados. English adjectives never change, so English never tells you who is speaking. In Portuguese, because the subject pronoun is often dropped, the adjective may be the only sign of whether the speaker is a man or a woman, just as obrigado and obrigada show it.

The form depends on the ending. Adjectives in -o have four forms: alto, alta, altos, altas. The vowel o is the masculine ending and a is the feminine, so an adjective in -e (inteligente, triste, doente) or in -z (feliz) has no gender ending to change and keeps one form for both genders. The plural adds -s after a vowel: altos, inteligentes. After z or r the plural adds a whole syllable, -es, because a bare z or r followed by s cannot be said, so feliz becomes felizes, and the same applies to nouns such as professor, professores. The written accent in simpático stays through simpática, simpáticos and simpáticas: the stress is on the same syllable in all four forms (the third from the end), and a stress of that kind is always marked.

Professions are nouns, and they agree with the person in the same way. Many end in -o and swap it for -a: médico, médica; engenheiro, engenheira; enfermeiro, enfermeira. Nouns in -or add -a: professor, professora. Nouns in -ante, such as estudante, have no feminine ending, so the article shows the gender: o estudante, a estudante. English has lost this for most jobs (a doctor is a doctor), keeping it only in a few words such as actor and actress. A mixed group takes the masculine plural: Eles são professores can describe men only, or men and women together.

A gente means we, but it is grammatically singular, so its verb is the third person singular. The adjective takes the gender of the real people: A gente está cansada if the group is women, A gente está cansado if it is men or mixed. The plural cansados is also heard in casual speech.

Muito before an adjective is an adverb meaning very, and an adverb never changes: muito cansada, muito cansados. Bem, mal, aqui and hoje are adverbs too, so Estou bem is the same for everyone. Muito also exists as an adjective meaning a lot of, and that one does agree, but it comes in a later lesson.

-or takes -a for the feminine; plural -es or -s
No gender form; the article shows the gender

grammar.title: Negation, yes or no answers and question words
grammar.explanation:
To make a sentence negative, put não directly before the verb: Eu não sou médico, Ela não está em casa. English needs the helper verb do for most negatives (I do not speak), but with to be it simply puts not after the verb (I am not). Portuguese puts não before the verb instead (Eu não sou), and needs no helper. The verb does not change and the other words stay where they were. When the subject is dropped, não still sits before the verb: Não estou cansado.

A yes or no question has the same words in the same order as a statement, and only the rising intonation and the question mark show it is a question. English inverts the order (You are tired becomes Are you tired?); Portuguese does not: Você está cansado? To answer yes, repeat the verb: Você é professor? Sou. Você está cansada? Estou, sim. This works because the verb ending already says who is acting, so the verb alone is a full answer. Sim by itself is also correct. To answer no, say Não, or Não, não sou, where the first não answers the question and the second negates the verb.

An interrogative word is a word that begins a question. Quem asks who, and expects a person. Como asks how, or what something is like. Onde asks where. O que asks what, and is literally the what. The question word comes first, and the verb usually comes next: Quem é ele? Onde você está? O que é isso? With a noun subject the verb often comes before it: Onde está o Carlos? With a pronoun subject the order Onde você está? is the common one. In casual speech the question word may also stay at the end, as in Você está onde? Isso is a pointing word like that: it does not change for gender or number and refers to something not yet named or to what was just said.

Compare Como ele é? and Como ele está? Word for word, both are how he is. The verb alone decides the meaning, and English has to use different phrases. Como ele é? uses ser, so it asks about what he is like, his character and looks: What is he like? Como ele está? uses estar, so it asks about his condition now: How is he? This is the same classifying versus condition choice as in the previous note, applied to a question.

rows: manner, or what something is like
[ˈõdʒi]: nasal on, d before final e is dj

examples.en: Are you a teacher? I am.

culture.title: Talking about how you feel in Brazil
culture.text:
When a Brazilian asks Tudo bem?, literally all well?, or Como você está?, the expected answer is usually short and positive: Tudo bem, Estou bem or just Tudo. But it is also normal to be honest about being tired, hungry or busy. People often say Tô cansado, with the shortened form of estou that you now know how to read, or Tô morrendo de fome, literally I am dying of hunger (morrendo is a verb form you will meet later; for now treat the whole phrase as one fixed expression), and another common answer is mais ou menos, literally more or less, meaning so-so. Brazilian conversation is warm, and sharing how you feel is a way to connect.

One word you will hear often is saudade, said sau-DA-dji. It describes missing someone or something, and there is no exact English translation. Estou com saudade de você means I miss you, and word for word it is I am with longing of you. It follows the same pattern as com fome and com sede: you are with the feeling, as a noun, so estar is the verb.

For professions, Brazilians often ask O que você faz?, literally what you do?, to find out someone's job (faz is a form of the verb fazer, to do or to make, which comes later; treat the question as a fixed formula for now), and you answer with ser and no article: Sou professor or Sou engenheira. Titles matter in some settings. Doutor and doutora are used for doctors and lawyers, and often for anyone in a professional role, even if the person does not have a doctorate. Professor and professora are also used as titles when speaking to a teacher directly, as in Bom dia, professora!

exercises.prompt: Why does está carry a written accent?
choices: It is stressed on the last syllable, which breaks the default for a word ending in a
Two words have fused into one
It shows that the e is closed
exercises.explanation: A word ending in a is stressed on the second to last syllable by default (ES-ta). Está is stressed on the last syllable, so the stressed vowel is marked, with an acute because the a is open. Without the accent, esta means this.

exercises.prompt: In estão, what does the tilde do?
choices: It makes the vowel nasal and also marks the stressed syllable
It shows that the word is a contraction
exercises.explanation: The tilde nasalizes the vowel. When a word has no other accent, the tilde also marks the stress, so es-TÃO needs nothing more.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means 'I am tired' (said by a man)?
exercises.explanation: Tiredness is a condition, not a classification, so use estar, and a man uses the masculine cansado.
A profession classifies the person, so it takes ser, and eu takes sou.
Tiredness is a condition she is in, so estar, and ela takes está.
The place of a person takes estar, and nós takes estamos.

exercises.prompt: Match the Portuguese with the English
Which sentence can only be said by a woman?
exercises.explanation: Ocupada is an adjective, so it agrees with the speaker and takes the feminine -a. Bem is an adverb and fome is a noun, so neither changes, and Sou professor uses the masculine form.

exercises.prompt: Why is the plural of feliz written felizes and not felizs?
choices: A word ending in z takes a whole extra syllable, -es, in the plural
The z changes into an s
exercises.explanation: After z or r, the plural adds the syllable -es, because a z followed directly by s cannot be said. Words ending in a vowel add only -s.

exercises.prompt: How many syllables does doente have, and why?
choices: Two, because oe is a diphthong
Three, because two strong vowels side by side never form a diphthong
Three, because the final e is silent
Two, because the n is silent
exercises.explanation: A diphthong needs a weak glide, an unstressed i or u, next to a strong vowel. The o and e of doente are both strong, so each has its own beat: do-EN-te.

exercises.prompt: How is the word triste said?
choices: TRIS-te, with a final e as in 'bed'
TRIS-tchi, with the final e said i and the t said tch
exercises.explanation: An unstressed final e is said i, and in most of Brazil a t before an i sound becomes tch.

choices: He is a happy person in general.
exercises.explanation: Estar describes a condition at a moment. Ele é feliz would classify him as a happy person.

exercises.prompt: What does 'Estou com fome' say word for word?
exercises.explanation: Com means with and fome is the noun hunger. Portuguese says you are with hunger; I am hungry is the natural English translation of the same idea.

exercises.prompt: In 'Elas estão muito cansadas', why is it muito and not muitas?
choices: Muito is an adverb modifying the adjective, and adverbs never agree
Muito agrees with estão, which is masculine
Muito ends in o, so it is always masculine
Elas takes the masculine form of muito
exercises.explanation: Muito here tells how much, and it modifies the adjective cansadas. Adverbs do not change for gender or number; only the adjective agrees with elas.

exercises.prompt: Why is it simpático with a written accent?
choices: It ends in o with the stress on the last syllable
It is stressed on the third syllable from the end, which no ending predicts
exercises.explanation: A word stressed on the third syllable from the end always carries an accent, because the ending rule cannot predict that stress. The a is open, so the accent is acute.

exercises.prompt: Which question asks what Rafael is like as a person?
exercises.explanation: Both como questions are literally how he is. Ser asks about what he is like, and estar asks how he is at the moment.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'Elas estão com sono' not change sono to sonas?
choices: Sono is a noun, and a noun after com does not agree with the subject
Feminine plural is never used with com
exercises.explanation: Only adjectives copy the gender and number of the subject. Sono is a noun, so it stays the same after com.

exercises.prompt: Why is tá written with an accent?
choices: It is a stressed word of one syllable ending in a, and such words are marked
It is stressed on the last syllable of a two-syllable word ending in a, like está
It is a contraction of two words
exercises.explanation: Tá is estar with its weak first syllable dropped, so one stressed syllable remains. A stressed one-syllable word ending in a, e or o is written with an accent; the a is open, so the mark is acute. Está has the accent for a different reason: it has two syllables and breaks the default for its ending.
Looking pretty on a particular day describes her condition at the moment, so estar. Ela é bonita would classify her as a pretty person.

exercises.hint_en: We are tired. (a group of women)
exercises.explanation: A gente means we but is grammatically singular, so the verb takes the form of ele and ela. Cansada agrees with the women in the group.
The place of an event takes ser, because where an event happens is part of what the event is. Estar is for the place of a person or object.

exercises.prompt: Why is it Sou professor, with no word for a, where English says I am a teacher?
choices: Professor is treated as a class the person belongs to, like an adjective, so no article is used
The article is dropped because the verb is ser
exercises.explanation: After ser, a profession names a class and works like an adjective, so no article is used. When the profession is described further, the article returns: Ela é uma médica simpática.
A profession takes ser, and eles takes são.
Não goes directly before the verb.
The adjective agrees with elas, which is feminine and plural, so cansadas.
Paula is one woman, so the adjective is feminine singular. The accent stays on the stressed syllable pá.
Asking who someone is asks for an identity, which takes ser.
Thirst is expressed with estar com plus the noun sede.
A condition takes estar, and a man uses the masculine cansado.
Não goes before the verb, a profession takes ser, and médica is feminine.
Hunger is expressed with estar com fome.
The place of a person takes estar. With a noun subject the verb often comes before it.

exercises.audio_pt: Eu não sou médico, sou engenheiro.
exercises.hint_en: I am not a doctor, I am an engineer.

exercises.audio_pt: Ela está em casa, mas está cansada.
exercises.hint_en: She is at home, but she is tired.

Match each word with the reason for its accent mark

pairs.en: Stressed on the last syllable of a word ending in a
Stressed on the last syllable of a word ending in o, with a closed o
Stressed on the third syllable from the end
The tilde marks the nasal sound and the stress
A stressed word of one syllable ending in o
